texts.0: SP, due to an instrument cross-check that stopped at the navigation display while the leg was flown, did not maintain the briefed cruising altitude and allowed the aircraft to drift more than 400 feet below the planned level. The trend was not recognized on the altimeter or on the vertical speed indicator at any point. IP had to intervene on the controls to arrest the descent and re-establish the aircraft at the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to head-down time spent on the chart and the stopwatch approaching the turning point, did not hold the briefed altitude within tolerance and reached 300 feet above the planned level. The deviation was corrected only after IP called the altitude twice, and level flight was re-established late in the following leg. SP did not detect the developing error from the altimeter without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged after the climb to the en route altitude, did not level off promptly and allowed the altitude to reach about 200 feet above the planned level. SP identified the deviation on the altimeter during the next cross-check cycle and returned to the briefed altitude within the same leg. The correction was made without prompting and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed cruising altitude within 150 feet throughout the route, with prompt and smooth corrections at each level-off. The altimeter cross-check was continuous and the deviations through the turning points remained inside tolerance. Altitude control was not disturbed by the navigation workload.
texts.4: SP flew the entire route with the altitude held to within a few tens of feet of the briefed level, including through the turning points and the deliberate altitude changes. Level-offs were anticipated and flown without overshoot. The altitude error at every checkpoint was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitude within standards, but the deviations were consistently on the low side of the briefed level and each correction began only after the altimeter had already moved appreciably. The trend is a cross-check that reaches the altimeter late, so errors are caught near the outer part of the tolerance rather than at onset. SP is expected to tighten the altimeter cross-check interval and to correct at the first indication of a trend on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the route with IP calling the altimeter cross-check interval needed to hold the briefed cruising altitude, due to this being one of the first cruise legs SP has flown holding a specific altitude against the navigation workload. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to tighten more of the cross-check interval independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the briefed cruising altitude to within 300 feet, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the altimeter cross-check interval being wider than the workload of the leg allowed for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to tighten the altimeter cross-check interval to match the leg workload.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed cruising altitude to about 210 feet, due to the power setting after a level-off being confirmed a beat after the cross-check rather than in the same interval. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm the power setting in the same cross-check interval as the level-off.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed cruising altitude to within 150 feet, due to a correction beginning a fraction after the altimeter first showed the trend rather than at the first indication. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to correct at the first indication of the trend, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the briefed cruising altitude to about 280 feet, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP maintained the briefed cruising altitude to about 200 feet throughout the route, with prompt and smooth corrections at each level-off and the altimeter cross-check continuous through the navigation workload. Correcting at the very first indication of a trend, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude cross-check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed cruising altitude to about 130 feet throughout the route, with the deviations through the turning points remaining inside tolerance and altitude control undisturbed by the navigation workload. The only refinement available was to hold that same cross-check rhythm through the busiest leg of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude cross-check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the entire route with altitude held to within a few tens of feet of the briefed level, including through the turning points and the deliberate altitude changes, level-offs anticipated and flown without overshoot with the altitude error at every checkpoint negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude cross-check discipline.

error_modes.label: AIRSPEED CONTROL AND POWER SETTING PER LEG

texts.0: SP, due to a power setting that was never adjusted after the change of altitude, did not hold the briefed leg IAS and allowed the airspeed to fall more than 25 knots below the planned value. The timing over the turning point was lost as a result and the remaining route had to be recomputed in flight. IP had to set the power and dictate the airspeed to recover the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a power setting selected from memory rather than computed for the altitude and wind of the leg, did not maintain the briefed IAS and reached 20 knots off the planned value. The airspeed was returned to the briefed figure only after IP pointed out the discrepancy on the airspeed indicator. The correction was delayed to the extent that the turning point was crossed off the calculated time.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction after a deliberate airspeed change, did not stabilize on the briefed leg IAS immediately and the airspeed remained about 15 knots off the planned value for part of the leg. SP identified the error against the flight plan card and reset the power without prompting, re-establishing the briefed IAS well before the turning point. Timing over the turning point was preserved.
texts.3: SP set the appropriate power settings for the altitude and wind of each leg and held the briefed IAS within 10 knots throughout the route. Deliberate airspeed changes were executed in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and stabilized on the new value without overshoot.
texts.4: SP held the leg IAS essentially on the briefed value throughout the route, with power set for the altitude and wind of each leg before any deviation could develop. Deliberate airspeed changes were flown in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and stabilized on the first attempt. The airspeed error at every checkpoint was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the leg IAS within standards, but the airspeed was held by frequent small power changes rather than by a power setting computed for the altitude and wind of the leg. The trend is a working airspeed that drifts toward the tolerance limit between corrections and demands continuous attention. SP is expected to compute and set the leg power setting immediately after roll-out on each heading during the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the route with IP calling the power setting computed for the altitude and wind of each leg, due to this being one of the first navigation legs SP has flown computing and setting leg power rather than adjusting it by feel. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to compute more of the leg power settings independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the leg IAS to within 20 knots of the briefed figure, at the limit of the standard, due to the power setting being adjusted repeatedly rather than computed once for the altitude and wind of the leg. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compute the power setting once for the leg rather than adjusting it repeatedly.
texts_at.2: SP held the briefed leg IAS to about 15 knots either side of the planned figure, due to the power setting being computed for the wind of the previous leg before it was refreshed for the new one. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to refresh the power computation for the wind of the new leg as the turn is rolled out.
texts_at.3: SP held the leg IAS to no more than 10 knots off the briefed figure, due to the computed power setting being applied a fraction after the roll-out rather than as part of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the computed power setting as part of the roll-out itself.

texts_above.1: SP held the briefed leg IAS to about 18 knots, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP set the appropriate power setting for the altitude and wind of the leg and held the briefed IAS to about 15 knots, deliberate airspeed changes executed in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and stabilized without overshoot. Applying the computed power setting as part of the roll-out, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound power-setting discipline.
texts_above.3: SP set the appropriate power setting for the altitude and wind of the leg and held the briefed IAS to about 8 knots, with the setting computed before any deviation could develop. The only refinement available was to hold that same precision through the fastest deliberate airspeed change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed power-setting discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the leg IAS essentially on the briefed value throughout the route, power set for the altitude and wind of each leg before any deviation could develop, deliberate airspeed changes flown in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and stabilized on the first attempt with the airspeed error at every checkpoint negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional power-setting discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to the wind correction angle never being applied to the planned heading, did not maintain the briefed heading and flew more than 15 degrees off the computed value for the whole leg. The accumulated track error placed the aircraft outside the intended corridor and the turning point could not be identified visually. IP had to assume the navigation and issue headings to regain the planned route.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete transition back to the instruments after the turn, did not roll out on the briefed heading and settled 10 degrees off the computed value. The heading was corrected only after IP called the discrepancy, and the aircraft remained off the planned track long enough to displace the turning point. SP did not cross-check the heading indicator against the flight plan card after roll-out.
texts.2: SP, due to an over-banked turn at the first turning point, did not roll out exactly on the briefed heading and stabilized about 8 degrees off the computed value. SP cross-checked the heading indicator against the flight plan card immediately after roll-out and re-established the briefed heading within a few seconds, without prompting. The track error was contained and the checkpoint was crossed as planned.
texts.3: SP held the briefed heading within 5 degrees on every leg, rolling out of each turn on the computed value with the wind correction angle applied for the leg. The heading was cross-checked against the flight plan card after every turn and the planned track was maintained between checkpoints.
texts.4: SP flew each leg essentially on the computed heading, with roll-outs on the exact value and the wind correction angle applied from the start of the leg. Track error at the checkpoints was negligible and no heading correction beyond one or two degrees was required at any point on the route.
texts.marginal: SP held the heading within standards, but the roll-outs were consistently a few degrees to one side and the error was left uncorrected until the checkpoint made it evident. The trend is a heading flown approximately rather than to the computed value, so track error accumulates over the length of the leg. SP is expected to roll out on the computed heading and verify it against the flight plan card immediately after every turn.

texts_at.0: SP flew the route legs with IP calling the wind correction angle and confirming the roll-out heading, due to this being one of the first navigation legs SP has flown correcting for wind on a computed heading. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to apply more of the wind correction angle independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the briefed heading to within 10 degrees, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the wind correction angle being applied a beat after roll-out rather than from the start of the leg. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply the wind correction angle from the start of the leg, not a beat after roll-out.
texts_at.2: SP held the briefed heading with excursions of up to 7 degrees, due to the heading indicator being cross-checked against the flight plan card a fraction after roll-out rather than immediately. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to cross-check the heading indicator against the flight plan card immediately after roll-out.
texts_at.3: SP held the briefed heading inside 5 degrees, due to the roll-out being confirmed against the computed value a moment after the turn rather than in the same motion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the roll-out against the computed value in the same motion as the turn.

texts_above.1: SP held the briefed heading to about 9 degrees, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP held the briefed heading to about 7 degrees on every leg, rolling out of each turn on the computed value with the wind correction angle applied for the leg and cross-checked against the flight plan card after every turn. Confirming the roll-out against the computed value in the same motion as the turn, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid heading roll-out discipline.
texts_above.3: SP held the briefed heading to about 4 degrees on every leg, with the wind correction angle applied and the planned track maintained between checkpoints. The only refinement available was to hold that same precision through the tightest turn of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed heading roll-out discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew each leg essentially on the computed heading, roll-outs on the exact value with the wind correction angle applied from the start of the leg, track error at the checkpoints negligible with no heading correction beyond one or two degrees required at any point on the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding heading roll-out discipline.

error_modes.label: IN-FLIGHT FUEL COMPUTATION AND PROFILE MANAGEMENT

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the fuel state during the working phase of the sortie, was not able to calculate the in-flight fuel accurately against time and distance and did not modify the mission profile in order not to violate the fuel restrictions. The fuel checks at the turning points were omitted and the remaining fuel was stated only when IP asked for it. IP had to terminate the route early and direct the recovery to keep the aircraft above the minimum fuel.
texts.1: SP, due to fuel checks made without reference to the time and distance remaining, calculated the in-flight fuel only to the lower limit of an acceptable figure and reached the briefed bingo fuel at the last turning point. The decision to shorten the profile was taken only after IP raised the fuel state twice. The recovery was flown on the minimum reserve, with no margin left for a delay.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial fuel calculation based on the planned rather than the actual ground speed, first produced a consumption figure that did not match the route remaining. SP recomputed the fuel against time and distance at the following checkpoint, recognized the shortfall unaided and dropped one leg from the profile to stay clear of the fuel restrictions. No prompting was required and the recovery was flown with the planned reserve intact.
texts.3: SP calculated the in-flight fuel accurately against time and distance at every checkpoint and compared it with the planned figures on the flight plan card. The profile was adjusted where required so that the fuel restrictions were not approached, and the recovery was commenced with the briefed reserve intact.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous and accurate fuel picture throughout the sortie, computing the fuel against time and distance ahead of each checkpoint and stating the projected recovery fuel before it was requested. The profile was managed so that the fuel remained above the planned figures at every point of the route. The difference between the computed and the actual reserve at landing was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP calculated the in-flight fuel within standards, but the checks were made at the checkpoints only and the figure was never projected forward to the recovery. The trend is a fuel picture that is correct for the present position while giving no early warning of a developing shortfall. SP is expected to project the fuel to the recovery point at every check and to name in advance the leg that would be dropped first on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP computed the in-flight fuel with IP calling the time and distance figures needed at each checkpoint, due to this being one of the first sorties SP has flown computing fuel against time and distance in flight rather than from a plan. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to compute more of the fuel checks independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP calculated the in-flight fuel accurately against time and distance at every checkpoint, due to the projection to the recovery point being made only at the final checkpoint rather than at each one. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to project the fuel to the recovery point at every checkpoint, not only the final one.
texts_at.2: SP calculated the in-flight fuel accurately against time and distance at every checkpoint, due to the leg that would be dropped first being identified only when asked rather than named in advance. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to name the leg that would be dropped first without waiting to be asked.
texts_at.3: SP calculated the in-flight fuel accurately against time and distance at every checkpoint, due to one fuel check being logged a moment after the checkpoint rather than at it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to log the fuel check at the checkpoint itself, not a moment after.

texts_above.1: SP calculated the in-flight fuel accurately against time and distance at every checkpoint. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP calculated the in-flight fuel accurately against time and distance at every checkpoint and compared it with the planned figures on the flight plan card, the profile adjusted where required so the fuel restrictions were never approached. Naming the leg to be dropped first without waiting to be asked would complete the projection discipline. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady fuel-projection discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained a continuous and accurate fuel picture through the sortie, computing the fuel against time and distance ahead of each checkpoint with the profile managed so the fuel remained above the planned figures at every point. The only refinement available was to state the projected recovery fuel a checkpoint earlier still. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate fuel-projection discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a continuous and accurate fuel picture throughout the sortie, computing the fuel against time and distance ahead of each checkpoint and stating the projected recovery fuel before it was requested, the difference between the computed and the actual reserve at landing negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary fuel-projection discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to the ground speed never being recomputed after the actual winds differed from the forecast, did not execute the deliberate airspeed changes required to be exactly above the turning points at the calculated time. The second turning point was crossed more than two minutes off the planned time and the error continued to grow along the route. IP had to compute the required airspeed and direct the changes to recover the timeline.
texts.1: SP, due to timing checks made only after each turning point had been passed, did not initiate the deliberate airspeed changes in time and arrived over the turning points at the limit of an acceptable timing error. The airspeed adjustments were made only after IP pointed out the accumulated delay. The timeline was restored late and only after successive corrections.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial ground speed check taken over too short a segment, first selected an airspeed change insufficient for the timing error. SP re-checked the elapsed time at the next visual checkpoint, computed the corrected airspeed in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and arrived over the following turning point at the calculated time. The correction was made without prompting.
texts.3: SP checked the elapsed time and ground speed at each checkpoint and executed deliberate airspeed changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual in order to be exactly above the turning points at the calculated time. The timing error at each turning point remained within a few seconds of the plan.
texts.4: SP managed the timeline with anticipation throughout the route, computing the required ground speed early in each leg and executing deliberate airspeed changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual before the timing error became apparent. Every turning point was crossed within seconds of the calculated time and the time over the terminal point was met exactly.
texts.marginal: SP arrived over the turning points within the required timing, but the corrections were large and applied close to the point rather than early in the leg. The trend is a timeline recovered by reacting at the checkpoint instead of by an airspeed change computed at the start of the leg. SP is expected to compute the required ground speed immediately after each turn and to apply the airspeed change at that point on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the route with IP calling the ground speed check and the airspeed change needed to correct the timing, due to this being one of the first navigation legs SP has flown computing an airspeed change to regain a calculated time. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to compute more of the airspeed changes independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP arrived over the turning points within about 50 seconds of the calculated time, at the edge of the standard, due to the ground speed check being taken only close to the point rather than immediately after the previous turn. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to check ground speed immediately after each turn, not close to the following point.
texts_at.2: SP arrived over the turning points within about 30 seconds of the calculated time, due to the airspeed change being computed a beat after the ground speed check rather than in the same step. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compute the airspeed change in the same step as the ground speed check.
texts_at.3: SP arrived over the turning points within about 10 seconds of the calculated time, due to the airspeed change being applied a fraction after it was computed rather than as it was computed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply the airspeed change as it is computed, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP arrived over the turning points within about 50 seconds of the calculated time, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP checked the elapsed time and ground speed at each checkpoint and executed deliberate airspeed changes early in the leg, arriving over the turning points within about 30 seconds of the calculated time. Applying the airspeed change as it is computed, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the timing further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable timing-anticipation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP checked the elapsed time and ground speed at each checkpoint and executed deliberate airspeed changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, the timing error at each turning point held within about 10 seconds of the plan. The only refinement available was to hold that same precision through the longest leg of the route. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good timing-anticipation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP managed the timeline with anticipation throughout the route, computing the required ground speed early in each leg and executing deliberate airspeed changes before the timing error became apparent, every turning point crossed within seconds of the calculated time with the time over the terminal point met exactly. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior timing-anticipation discipline.

error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CHANGE TECHNIQUE AND IN-FLIGHT PROCEDURES

texts.0: SP, due to incomplete knowledge of the flight altitude change procedures of the Techniques and Procedures Manual, did not execute the planned altitude changes with the prescribed technique and did not execute all required in-flight procedures. The climb was initiated without the power and attitude called for by the manual, and the fuel, systems and position checks for the leg were left undone. IP had to direct the profile and personally complete the in-flight procedures.
texts.1: SP, due to the in-flight procedures being recalled item by item instead of being flown as a flow, executed the altitude changes with a technique that only just met the requirement and completed the checks at the limit of an acceptable standard. Each remaining procedure was carried out after IP prompted for it. The checks for one leg were finished only after the following turning point had been crossed.
texts.2: SP, due to a climb initiated before the power was set for the new altitude, first executed an altitude change that did not follow the technique of the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP recognized the deviation, reset power and attitude and completed the level-off correctly, then carried out the remaining in-flight procedures for the leg without prompting and in the correct order. No IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP executed the flight altitude changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with power and attitude set for the climb or descent and a controlled level-off at the new altitude. All required in-flight procedures were executed at the planned points and in the correct sequence.
texts.4: SP executed every altitude change exactly as prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with the level-offs anticipated and flown without overshoot. All required in-flight procedures were completed ahead of the planned points and integrated into the navigation task without any disturbance to aircraft control. Deviations from the prescribed technique were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP executed the altitude changes and the in-flight procedures within standards, but the procedures were completed at the end of each leg rather than at the planned points, so several tasks accumulated near the turning points. The trend is a workload pushed into the busiest part of the route, where the aircraft control task is already highest. SP is expected to distribute the in-flight procedures across the leg and complete each one at its planned point on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP executed the altitude changes with IP calling the power and attitude needed for the climb or descent and confirming each in-flight procedure, due to this being one of the first sorties SP has flown running the full altitude-change technique and procedure flow. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to run more of the altitude-change technique independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP executed the flight altitude changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, due to one in-flight procedure being completed at the end of the leg rather than at its own planned point, so the level-off that followed was flown with the scan still divided and each new altitude was settled on within 300 feet, at the edge of the standard. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete each in-flight procedure at its own planned point, not at the end of the leg.
texts_at.2: SP executed the flight altitude changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, due to two procedures being run together near the turning point rather than spaced across the leg, so the altitude change through the turn was flown with the scan divided and each new altitude was settled on no more than 210 feet from the assigned level. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to space the procedures across the leg rather than running them together near the turn.
texts_at.3: SP executed the flight altitude changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, due to one procedure being completed a fraction after its planned point rather than at it, so the rate was reduced a fraction behind the lead point and each new altitude was settled on up to 150 feet from the assigned level. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to complete each procedure exactly at its planned point, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP executed the flight altitude changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP executed the flight altitude changes in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, power and attitude set for the climb or descent with all required in-flight procedures executed at the planned points and in the correct sequence. Completing the one late procedure exactly at its planned point, rather than a fraction after, would even out the workload further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured procedure-distribution discipline.
texts_above.3: SP executed every altitude change exactly as prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual, level-offs anticipated and flown without overshoot with the in-flight procedures distributed across the leg rather than concentrated near the turn. The only refinement available was to distribute that same discipline through the busiest leg of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise procedure-distribution discipline.
texts_above.4: SP executed every altitude change exactly as prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual, level-offs anticipated and flown without overshoot, all required in-flight procedures completed ahead of the planned points and integrated into the navigation task without any disturbance to aircraft control with deviations from the prescribed technique negligible. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate procedure-distribution discipline.

error_modes.label: WINGMAN CONSIDERATION - FORMATION POSITION WHILE NAVIGATING

texts.0: SP, due to attention captured by the chart and the stopwatch while the aircraft state went unmonitored, did not maintain the briefed formation position while flying the route and allowed the aircraft to close inside the briefed lateral limit. The corresponding Formation criteria applied to this sortie were not met and the position error was not recognized by SP at any stage. IP had to take control and move the aircraft back out to a safe position.
texts.1: SP, due to the navigation task being worked head-down for extended periods, did not hold the briefed formation position while flying the route and reached the outer limit of the position acceptable under the Formation criteria applied to this sortie. Line, spacing and step-down were corrected only after successive radio calls from lead. The position was restored slowly and drifted again as soon as the next navigation check was started.
texts.2: SP, due to a power correction applied late after lead's turn at the first turning point, did not hold the briefed spacing and opened outside the planned position for part of the leg. SP detected the error visually, corrected line and spacing with smooth power and bank inputs and re-established the briefed position without any call from lead or IP. Aircraft control remained steady throughout the correction.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed formation position throughout the route while carrying out the navigation task, holding line, spacing and step-down in accordance with the corresponding Formation criteria applied to this sortie. Position corrections were small and smooth and were made without any call from lead.
texts.4: SP held the briefed formation position throughout the route with negligible variation, dividing attention between lead and the navigation task without either being neglected. Line, spacing and step-down were maintained through the turns and the altitude changes. Every correction was anticipated from lead's aircraft rather than made in reaction to it.
texts.marginal: SP held the formation position within standards, but the position was maintained in bursts, tightening each time SP looked out and drifting while the navigation task was worked head-down. The trend is a visual scan that leaves lead unmonitored for too long at a time, so the position is recovered rather than held. SP is expected to break the navigation task into shorter head-down periods and to keep a continuous reference on lead during the next formation navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the formation position while navigating with IP calling when to return the reference to lead between navigation checks, due to this being one of the first formation navigation legs SP has flown dividing attention between lead and the route. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to hold more of the reference on lead independently between checks on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the briefed formation position while flying the route, at the edge of the standard, due to one head-down period on the navigation task running long enough that the position had to be recovered afterward. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to shorten every head-down period so the position never needs recovering.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed formation position while flying the route, due to the reference on lead being picked up a beat after the navigation task ended rather than held through it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold a continuous reference on lead through the navigation task, not pick it up after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed formation position while flying the route, due to one correction being made a fraction after the position had drifted rather than as it began to drift. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to correct the position as it begins to drift, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the briefed formation position while flying the route. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP maintained the briefed formation position throughout the route while carrying out the navigation task, holding line, spacing and step-down in accordance with the corresponding Formation criteria with position corrections small and smooth and made without any call from lead. Correcting the position as it begins to drift, rather than a fraction after, would smooth the hold further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent formation-position discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed formation position throughout the route while carrying out the navigation task, position corrections small and smooth and made without any call from lead with the reference on lead held continuously. The only refinement available was to hold that same continuous reference through the busiest navigation task of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined formation-position discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed formation position throughout the route with negligible variation, dividing attention between lead and the navigation task without either being neglected, line, spacing and step-down maintained through the turns and the altitude changes with every correction anticipated from lead's aircraft rather than made in reaction to it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless formation-position discipline.

error_modes.label: TRIM NOT SET AFTER LEVEL-OFF AND POWER CHANGES

texts.0: SP, due to the aircraft being left out of trim after the level-off at the en route altitude, did not re-trim for the cruise condition and flew the first leg against continuous stick pressure. The altitude wandered more than 400 feet from the briefed level and the aircraft drifted more than 15 degrees off the planned track before any correction was attempted. The standing control pressure and the resulting uneven fuel flow were not recognized by SP at any stage. IP had to take the controls, trim the aircraft and re-establish it on altitude and heading.
texts.1: SP, due to poor trim carried from the departure into the first en route leg, did not set the trim for the cruise power setting and continued to fly the leg against residual control pressure. Altitude excursions reached 300 feet and the heading wandered up to 10 degrees either side of the planned track. Trim was set only after IP called for it twice, and the same pattern reappeared after the next power change.
texts.2: SP, due to trim not being reset after the power reduction at level-off, did not remove the residual stick pressure and allowed the altitude to drift about 200 feet with a heading error of some 7 degrees. SP recognized the standing control pressure during the cross-check, trimmed the aircraft and re-established the leg parameters within the same leg. No prompting from IP was required.
texts.3: SP trimmed the aircraft immediately after the level-off and re-trimmed after each power change on the route, so altitude stayed within 150 feet and heading within 5 degrees of the planned values. Control pressures were kept off the stick and the fuel flow remained even. Trim was checked again after each turning point.
texts.4: SP kept the aircraft in trim throughout the route, re-trimming after every power and altitude change before any deviation could develop. Altitude and heading were held with negligible error and the fuel flow remained steady across the whole leg structure. Cockpit workload stayed low because the aircraft was stabilized by trim rather than by control pressure.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude and heading inside standards, but the aircraft was flown with residual control pressure and trim was set only after the deviation had become visible on the instruments. The trend is trim used as a correction instead of as the means of stabilizing the leg, which leaves the errors near the outer part of tolerance and increases fatigue over a long route. SP is expected to trim immediately after each level-off and power change on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP trimmed the aircraft with IP calling when to retrim after the level-off and after each power change, due to this being one of the first cruise legs SP has flown trimming the aircraft as the primary means of stabilizing rather than holding pressure. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to retrim more of the level-offs and power changes independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP trimmed the aircraft after the level-off, holding altitude to about 300 feet and heading to about 10 degrees, at the edge of the standard, due to the trim being set only once the residual pressure had become clearly noticeable. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim immediately after the level-off, not once pressure becomes noticeable.
texts_at.2: SP trimmed the aircraft after the level-off, holding altitude to about 210 feet and heading to about 7 degrees, due to the retrim after a power change lagging the change by a beat rather than following it immediately. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to retrim immediately after every power change, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP trimmed the aircraft after the level-off, holding altitude to about 150 feet and heading to about 5 degrees, due to the trim check after a turning point coming a fraction after the roll-out rather than at it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the trim at the roll-out itself, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP trimmed the aircraft after the level-off, holding altitude to about 280 feet and heading to about 9 degrees, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP trimmed the aircraft immediately after the level-off and re-trimmed after each power change on the route, altitude held to about 200 feet and heading to about 7 degrees with control pressures kept off the stick and the fuel flow even. Checking the trim at the roll-out itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to good trim discipline.
texts_above.3: SP trimmed the aircraft immediately after the level-off and re-trimmed after each power change on the route, altitude held to about 130 feet and heading to about 4 degrees, trim checked again after each turning point. The only refinement available was to hold that same trim discipline through the longest leg of the route. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good trim discipline.
texts_above.4: SP kept the aircraft in trim throughout the route, re-trimming after every power and altitude change before any deviation could develop, altitude and heading held with negligible error and fuel flow remaining steady with cockpit workload low because the aircraft was stabilized by trim rather than by control pressure. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent trim discipline.

error_modes.label: CLEARING PRIORITY - CHART READ DOWN IN THE COCKPIT INSTEAD OF AT EYE LEVEL
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d ROUTE BASICS - MISSION ELEMENT PRIORITIES

texts.0: SP, due to the chart being read down in the cockpit instead of being brought up to eye level, did not keep the required share of route time heads up and eyes out and abandoned the outside scan for long uninterrupted periods. Clearing, which is the highest priority task on the route, was displaced by the chart work while the altitude ran more than 400 feet from the briefed level and the track error grew unchecked. Neither the loss of lookout nor the developing deviation was recognized by SP. IP had to intervene to restore the visual scan and to re-establish the aircraft parameters.
texts.1: SP, due to chart reading performed low in the cockpit rather than at eye level, did not keep close to eighty percent of the route time heads up and eyes out and interrupted the outside scan for long blocks at a time. Altitude reached 300 feet from the briefed level and the heading up to 10 degrees off the planned track during those blocks. The lookout and the parameters were restored only after repeated calls from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the chart being held low for the first checkpoint identification, did not bring it up to eye level and lost the outside scan for a noticeable period, with the altitude drifting about 200 feet and the heading about 7 degrees. SP recognized the deficiency, raised the chart to eye level for the remaining checkpoints and re-established the parameters without prompting. Clearing was thereafter given priority over the chart work.
texts.3: SP brought the chart up to eye level for every identification, kept the greater part of the route time heads up and eyes out and returned the focus to clearing outside after each check. Altitude stayed within 150 feet and heading within 5 degrees while the chart was being used. The navigation tasks were fitted around the lookout rather than the reverse.
texts.4: SP kept the chart at eye level throughout and interleaved short glances with a continuous outside scan, so clearing was never displaced by the navigation task. Altitude and heading remained essentially on the planned values during every identification. Checkpoint work was completed with no perceptible loss of visual lookout.
texts.marginal: SP held the required parameters within standards and did raise the chart, but the identifications were still worked as long single looks with the chart low in the cockpit before being corrected. The trend is a chart technique that concentrates head-down time instead of breaking it into short glances at eye level, so both clearing and the flown parameters degrade toward the edge of tolerance in the seconds before each checkpoint. SP is expected to keep the chart at eye level and to return the focus outside between glances on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP identified checkpoints on the chart with IP calling when to bring the chart up to eye level and when to return the scan outside, due to this being one of the first navigation legs SP has flown identifying checkpoints while keeping clearing as the first priority. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to bring more of the chart to eye level independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP brought the chart up to eye level for identification, holding altitude to within 300 feet and heading to within 10 degrees during the identification, at the edge of the standard, due to one identification being worked as a long single look before the chart was raised. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to bring the chart to eye level from the start of every identification, not after a long look.
texts_at.2: SP brought the chart up to eye level for identification, holding altitude to about 210 feet and heading to about 7 degrees during the identification, due to the focus returning outside a beat after the identification rather than in short glances through it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to return the focus outside in short glances through the identification, not only after it.
texts_at.3: SP brought the chart up to eye level for identification, holding altitude to within 150 feet and heading to within 5 degrees during the identification, due to one glance running a fraction longer than the rest before the focus returned outside. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold every glance to the same short length as the rest.

texts_above.1: SP brought the chart up to eye level for identification, holding altitude to about 280 feet and heading to about 9 degrees during the identification, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP brought the chart up to eye level for every identification, altitude held to about 200 feet and heading to about 7 degrees while the chart was being used, the navigation tasks fitted around the lookout rather than the reverse. Holding every glance to the same short length, rather than the one that ran long, would sharpen the scan further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sound chart-at-eye-level discipline.
texts_above.3: SP brought the chart up to eye level for every identification, altitude held to about 130 feet and heading to about 4 degrees while the chart was being used, clearing never displaced by the navigation task. The only refinement available was to hold that same short-glance discipline through the busiest identification of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sure-handed chart-at-eye-level discipline.
texts_above.4: SP kept the chart at eye level throughout and interleaved short glances with a continuous outside scan, altitude and heading remaining essentially on the planned values during every identification with checkpoint work completed with no perceptible loss of visual lookout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional chart-at-eye-level discipline.

error_modes.label: TASKS PERFORMED DURING TURNS INSTEAD OF FLYING THE AIRCRAFT AND CLEARING
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d(8)(g)-(h) BIG PICTURE AND ALTITUDE CONTROL

texts.0: SP, due to cockpit tasks continued through the turn at the turning point instead of flying the aircraft and clearing and doing nothing else, did not maintain terrain and traffic clearing where it is most critical and did not control the aircraft in the turn. The bank was allowed to steepen with the altitude running more than 400 feet below the briefed level and the roll-out more than 15 degrees off the new leg heading. The descent in the turn was not recognized by SP from the altimeter or the attitude indicator. IP had to take the controls to stop the descent and complete the roll-out on the planned track.
texts.1: SP, due to the fuel check and the log entry being worked inside the turn rather than after the roll-out, did not give the turn the undivided attention required and allowed the aircraft to descend 300 feet while banked. The roll-out finished 10 degrees off the new leg heading and the aircraft was re-established only after IP called both the altitude and the heading. The same task loading was carried into the following turn.
texts.2: SP, due to a chart check started before the roll-out was complete, did not keep the scan on aircraft control and clearing through the turn and lost about 200 feet with a roll-out error of some 7 degrees. SP recognized the deviation on the altimeter, deferred the remaining cockpit tasks until wings level and re-established altitude and heading inside the leg. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew each turn at the turning points with the attention on aircraft control and clearing only, deferring the chart, fuel and log tasks until after the roll-out. Altitude was held within 150 feet through the turns and the roll-out was within 5 degrees of the new leg heading. Terrain clearance was visually assessed before and during each turn.
texts.4: SP protected every turn from cockpit tasks, cleared the flight path into the turn and rolled out on the planned heading with negligible altitude loss. The navigation work was sequenced entirely into the straight segments where it belonged. Turns were flown as a discrete task from entry to roll-out.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude and roll-out heading within standards through the turning points, but cockpit tasks were still being carried into the first part of each turn and only set aside once the bank was established. The trend is task loading that overlaps the most critical phase of the route, so the deviations grow through the turn and are recovered after the roll-out rather than prevented. SP is expected to complete or defer all cockpit tasks before initiating the turn on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turns at the turning points with IP calling when to defer cockpit tasks until the roll-out, due to this being one of the first navigation legs SP has flown protecting the turn from cockpit tasks. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to defer more of the cockpit tasks independently through the turn on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP flew each turn at the turning points with attention on aircraft control and clearing, holding altitude to about 300 feet through the turn and rolling out within about 10 degrees of the new leg heading, at the edge of the standard, due to a cockpit task being carried into the first part of the turn before it was deferred. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to defer every cockpit task before, not into, the first part of the turn.
texts_at.2: SP flew each turn at the turning points with attention on aircraft control and clearing, holding altitude to about 210 feet through the turn and rolling out within about 7 degrees of the new leg heading, due to a chart check being started a beat before the roll-out was complete. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start the chart check only after the roll-out is complete, not a beat before.
texts_at.3: SP flew each turn at the turning points with attention on aircraft control and clearing, holding altitude to about 150 feet through the turn and rolling out within about 5 degrees of the new leg heading, due to one cockpit task being resumed a fraction before wings level rather than at it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to resume cockpit tasks exactly at wings level, not a fraction before.

texts_above.1: SP flew each turn at the turning points with attention on aircraft control and clearing, holding altitude to about 280 feet through the turn and rolling out within about 9 degrees of the new leg heading, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew each turn at the turning points with the attention on aircraft control and clearing only, deferring the chart, fuel and log tasks until after the roll-out, altitude held within about 200 feet through the turns and the roll-out within about 7 degrees of the new leg heading. Resuming cockpit tasks exactly at wings level, rather than a fraction before, would sharpen the turn discipline further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid turn-protection discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew each turn at the turning points with the attention on aircraft control and clearing only, altitude held within about 130 feet through the turns and the roll-out within about 4 degrees of the new leg heading, terrain clearance visually assessed before and during each turn. The only refinement available was to hold that same discipline through the tightest turn of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed turn-protection discipline.
texts_above.4: SP protected every turn from cockpit tasks, clearing the flight path into the turn and rolling out on the planned heading with negligible altitude loss, the navigation work sequenced entirely into the straight segments where it belonged with turns flown as a discrete task from entry to roll-out. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding turn-protection discipline.

error_modes.label: BIG PICTURE - ALTIMETER NOT CROSSCHECKED AGAINST KNOWN ELEVATIONS
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d(8)(g)-(h) BIG PICTURE AND ALTITUDE CONTROL

texts.0: SP, due to an altimeter that was never crosschecked against the known elevation of towers, lakes, airfields and peak elevations along the route, did not verify the actual height above the ground and did not use the major terrain features to keep the big picture. The aircraft was flown more than 400 feet from the briefed level with the positional awareness lost, and no climb was initiated although the route structure allowed it and the position was in doubt. IP had to intervene to re-establish the aircraft and to re-orientate the flight on the route.
texts.1: SP, due to the height above the ground being assessed from the altimeter alone without any crosscheck against the elevations of known features, did not detect the developing error and reached 300 feet from the briefed level with the track wandering up to 10 degrees. The major terrain features abeam the leg were not used for positional awareness and the doubt about position was allowed to persist. Both the altitude and the orientation were resolved only after IP prompted the crosscheck.
texts.2: SP, due to a visual assessment of the height above the ground that was not backed by a crosscheck of the altimeter against a known lake and airfield elevation, did not confirm the level early and drifted about 200 feet with a heading error of some 7 degrees. SP used the next major terrain feature to re-establish the big picture, checked the altimeter against its known elevation and returned to the briefed profile without prompting. The remaining legs were flown with the crosscheck restored.
texts.3: SP used the major terrain features along the route to maintain positional awareness and crosschecked the altimeter against the known elevations of the features passed. Altitude was held within 150 feet and the track within 5 degrees, and the intention to climb early if the position became doubtful was stated. The big picture was retained through every leg change.
texts.4: SP maintained the big picture continuously from the major terrain features, confirming each with the known elevation against the altimeter and keeping the height above the ground visually assessed. Altitude and track error at each checkpoint were negligible and the position was never in doubt. Where the route structure allowed it, altitude was used deliberately to make the visual navigation easier.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitude and the track inside standards and did use the terrain features, but the crosscheck against known elevations was made only at the checkpoints and not between them. The trend is positional awareness that is rebuilt at each fix rather than carried continuously, so any error between checkpoints grows to the edge of tolerance before it is detected. SP is expected to crosscheck the altimeter against known elevations along the leg and to climb early when the position is in doubt on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP used the major terrain features along the route with IP naming which feature to crosscheck the altimeter against, due to this being one of the first navigation legs SP has flown crosschecking the altimeter against known terrain elevations. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to crosscheck more of the terrain features independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP used the major terrain features along the route to maintain positional awareness, holding altitude to within 300 feet and track to within 10 degrees, at the edge of the standard, due to the altimeter crosscheck against a known elevation being made only at the checkpoint rather than along the leg. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to crosscheck the altimeter against known elevations along the leg, not only at the checkpoint.
texts_at.2: SP used the major terrain features along the route to maintain positional awareness, holding altitude to about 210 feet and track to about 7 degrees, due to the big picture being rebuilt a beat after a feature passed rather than carried continuously through it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to carry the big picture continuously through each feature, not rebuild it after.
texts_at.3: SP used the major terrain features along the route to maintain positional awareness, holding altitude to within 150 feet and track to within 5 degrees, due to the height above ground being assessed a fraction after the feature was abeam rather than as it passed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to assess the height above ground as the feature passes, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP used the major terrain features along the route to maintain positional awareness, holding altitude to about 280 feet and track to about 9 degrees, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP used the major terrain features along the route to maintain positional awareness and crosschecked the altimeter against the known elevations of the features passed, altitude held to about 200 feet and track to about 7 degrees with the big picture retained through every leg change. Assessing the height above ground as each feature passes, rather than a fraction after, would sharpen the crosscheck further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to steady terrain-crosscheck discipline.
texts_above.3: SP used the major terrain features along the route to maintain positional awareness and crosschecked the altimeter against the known elevations of the features passed, altitude held to about 130 feet and track to about 4 degrees with the intention to climb early stated whenever position became doubtful. The only refinement available was to hold that same crosscheck rhythm through the longest gap between features. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate terrain-crosscheck discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained the big picture continuously from the major terrain features, confirming each with the known elevation against the altimeter and keeping the height above the ground visually assessed, altitude and track error at each checkpoint negligible with the position never in doubt and altitude used deliberately where the route structure allowed it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary terrain-crosscheck discipline.

error_modes.label: COCKPIT TASKS STARTED BEFORE STABILIZING IN ROUTE POSITION

texts.0: SP, due to the radio channel change and the in-flight checks being started before stabilizing in route position, did not establish the briefed two to four ship widths spacing before diverting attention inside the cockpit. The aircraft closed well inside the route limits with the flight path not deconflicted from Number 1 and the altitude running more than 400 feet from the briefed level. Neither the closure nor the altitude trend was recognized by SP while the attention was inside. IP had to take the controls and move the aircraft back out to a safe position.
texts.1: SP, due to attention diverted to the in-flight checks before the aircraft was stabilized in route, did not hold the briefed spacing and drifted out toward the route formation's outer spacing limit while the altitude reached 300 feet from the briefed level. Position and altitude were restored only after successive calls from Number 1 and from IP. The same sequence was repeated at the next radio channel change.
texts.2: SP, due to a fuel check begun while still moving out from close position, did not stabilize in route first and allowed the spacing and the altitude to open by some 200 feet before the check was interrupted. SP recognized the deviation, stabilized in route at the briefed spacing and then completed the check without any call from Number 1. Aircraft control remained steady throughout.
texts.3: SP stabilized in route position at the briefed spacing before every radio change, in-flight check and cockpit task, and held altitude within 150 feet while the task was worked. The specific route position was maintained rather than the wide tolerance being used as a target. Attention was returned outside between each cockpit action.
texts.4: SP moved to route and stabilized at the briefed spacing automatically before each cockpit task, so no task was ever worked from an unstable position. Spacing, stack and altitude showed negligible variation while the radio changes and in-flight checks were completed. Number 1 was kept in sight continuously throughout every task.
texts.marginal: SP kept spacing and altitude within standards, but several cockpit tasks were begun while the aircraft was still settling into route rather than after it was stabilized. The trend is a task started on an unstable position, so the spacing opens or closes toward the limits before the task is finished and is then recovered. SP is expected to stabilize in route at the briefed spacing before diverting attention to any cockpit task on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP moved to route position with IP calling when the spacing had stabilized before any cockpit task began, due to this being one of the first formation navigation legs SP has flown stabilizing in route before starting a cockpit task. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to confirm more of the stabilized spacing independently before starting a task on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP stabilized in route position at the briefed spacing before diverting attention inside, holding altitude to about 300 feet while the task was worked, at the edge of the standard, due to one cockpit task being started while the aircraft was still settling into route rather than after it stabilized. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to wait for the aircraft to stabilize in route before starting any cockpit task.
texts_at.2: SP stabilized in route position at the briefed spacing before diverting attention inside, holding altitude to about 210 feet while the task was worked, due to the confirmation of stable spacing coming a beat after the task had already started. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm stable spacing before, not after, the task has started.
texts_at.3: SP stabilized in route position at the briefed spacing before diverting attention inside, holding altitude to about 150 feet while the task was worked, due to attention returning outside a fraction after the task ended rather than as it ended. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to return attention outside in the same motion the task ends.

texts_above.1: SP stabilized in route position at the briefed spacing before diverting attention inside, holding altitude to about 280 feet while the task was worked, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP stabilized in route position at the briefed spacing before every radio change, in-flight check and cockpit task, altitude held to about 200 feet while the task was worked with the specific route position maintained rather than the wide tolerance used as a target. Returning attention outside in the same motion a task ends, rather than a fraction after, would smooth the sequence further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to dependable route-stabilization discipline.
texts_above.3: SP stabilized in route position at the briefed spacing before every cockpit task, altitude held to about 130 feet while the task was worked with attention returned outside between each cockpit action. The only refinement available was to hold that same stabilization discipline through the busiest task of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to notably good route-stabilization discipline.
texts_above.4: SP moved to route and stabilized at the briefed spacing automatically before each cockpit task, so no task was ever worked from an unstable position, spacing, stack and altitude showing negligible variation while the radio changes and in-flight checks were completed with Number 1 kept in sight continuously throughout every task. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior route-stabilization discipline.

error_modes.label: CLOSE FORMATION - MORE THAN ONE REFERENCE CORRECTED AT A TIME

texts.0: SP, due to an attempt to correct stack, fore and aft position and lateral spacing simultaneously instead of one reference at a time, did not re-establish the close position and drove the aircraft through the briefed wingtip separation with the flight path not deconflicted from Number 1. The combined stick, bank and power inputs produced an oscillation in which the altitude also ran more than 400 feet from the briefed level. The deteriorating position was not recognized by SP as an over-controlled correction. IP had to take the controls and move the aircraft out to a safe position.
texts.1: SP, due to simultaneous corrections applied to more than one fingertip reference, did not correct in the order stack first, fore and aft second and lateral spacing last, so each input disturbed the reference just corrected. The position was held only at the outer limit acceptable for the sortie and the airspeed swung up to 20 knots during the corrections. The aircraft was stabilized only after repeated calls from Number 1 and from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to lateral spacing and stack being worked together after a deviation was recognized, did not correct one reference at a time and allowed the position to wander with airspeed excursions of about 15 knots. SP recognized the over-controlling, returned to the sequence of stack, then fore and aft, then lateral spacing, and re-established the position without any call. The remaining corrections were made in the correct order.
texts.3: SP corrected one reference at a time in the order stack, fore and aft, then lateral spacing, using continuous, small and controlled inputs. Airspeed excursions during the corrections stayed within 10 knots and the position was re-established promptly each time. Deviations were recognized early and the required inputs were anticipated.
texts.4: SP held the close position with corrections so small and so early that no single reference was ever allowed to develop a visible error. The sequence stack, fore and aft, lateral spacing was applied instinctively and the airspeed remained essentially constant throughout. Position was maintained rather than recovered.
texts.marginal: SP held the close position within standards, but corrections were still applied to two references at once before the sequence was re-imposed, and each recovery took longer than it needed to. The trend is a correction technique that mixes stack, fore and aft and lateral inputs, so the position drifts to the edge of tolerance before it settles. SP is expected to correct one reference at a time in the published order on the next formation navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP corrected the fingertip references with IP calling the order stack, fore and aft, lateral spacing for each correction, due to this being one of the first formation legs SP has flown correcting one reference at a time in the published order. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to hold more of the published correction order independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP corrected one reference at a time in the order stack, fore and aft, lateral spacing, holding airspeed excursions to about 20 knots during the corrections, at the edge of the standard, due to two references being worked together before the published order was re-imposed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to correct one reference at a time from the start, not re-impose the order after two are worked together.
texts_at.2: SP corrected one reference at a time in the order stack, fore and aft, lateral spacing, holding airspeed excursions to about 15 knots during the corrections, due to the lateral reference being started a beat before the stack had fully settled. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to start the lateral reference only after the stack has fully settled.
texts_at.3: SP corrected one reference at a time in the order stack, fore and aft, lateral spacing, holding airspeed excursions to about 10 knots during the corrections, due to the fore-and-aft reference being addressed a fraction before the stack was fully confirmed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to confirm the stack fully before addressing the fore-and-aft reference.

texts_above.1: SP corrected one reference at a time in the order stack, fore and aft, lateral spacing, holding airspeed excursions to about 18 knots during the corrections, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP corrected one reference at a time in the order stack, fore and aft, then lateral spacing, using continuous, small and controlled inputs, airspeed excursions during the corrections held to about 15 knots with the position re-established promptly each time. Confirming the stack fully before the fore-and-aft reference, rather than a fraction before, would tighten the sequence further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured correction-sequencing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP corrected one reference at a time in the published order, airspeed excursions during the corrections held to about 8 knots with deviations recognized early and the required inputs anticipated. The only refinement available was to hold that same sequencing through the busiest correction of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise correction-sequencing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the close position with corrections so small and so early that no single reference was ever allowed to develop a visible error, the sequence stack, fore and aft, lateral spacing applied instinctively with airspeed remaining essentially constant throughout and the position maintained rather than recovered. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate correction-sequencing discipline.

error_modes.label: CHASING THE POWER - OVER CORRECTION OF POWER IN POSITION

texts.0: SP, due to over correction of power in which the PCL was moved with the whole arm instead of small movements of the wrist, did not use one movement to start the correction, one to stop the aircraft and one to stabilize it, and ended up chasing the power. The resulting fore and aft oscillation carried airspeed swings of more than 25 knots and drove the aircraft through the briefed fore and aft limits relative to Number 1. The divergent oscillation was not recognized by SP as a power problem. IP had to take the controls and stabilize the aircraft clear of Number 1.
texts.1: SP, due to power corrections applied in large movements rather than the three deliberate PCL movements required, did not stop the aircraft at the reference and continued to chase the power along the fore and aft axis. Airspeed excursions reached 20 knots and the position was held only at the outer limit acceptable for the sortie. The oscillation was damped only after repeated calls from IP to set a power setting and leave it.
texts.2: SP, due to a power correction that was not followed by a movement to stop the aircraft, did not arrest the closure at the reference and overshot the fore and aft position with an airspeed excursion of about 15 knots. SP recognized the over correction, applied the stopping and stabilizing PCL movements and settled the aircraft back on the reference without prompting. Subsequent corrections were made with small wrist movements.
texts.3: SP corrected fore and aft position with the three PCL movements, one to start the correction, one to stop the aircraft and one to stabilize it, keeping airspeed excursions within 10 knots. Power was changed with small movements of the wrist rather than the whole arm. The aircraft settled on the reference without overshoot.
texts.4: SP anticipated the power required and made corrections so small that the fore and aft reference never developed a visible error, with airspeed effectively constant.
