Every correction was started, stopped and stabilized deliberately, and no chasing of the power occurred at any stage of the route. Cockpit workload remained low throughout the formation legs.
texts.marginal: SP kept fore and aft position and airspeed within standards, but the stopping movement was frequently late so each correction ended with a small overshoot and a second input. The trend is a power technique that starts corrections well but does not stop them, leaving the airspeed near the outer part of tolerance during every adjustment. SP is expected to use the three deliberate PCL movements with wrist inputs only on the next formation navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP corrected fore and aft position with IP calling the three PCL movements, one to start, one to stop and one to stabilize, due to this being one of the first formation legs SP has flown correcting power with the three deliberate PCL movements rather than a single input. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to make more of the three PCL movements independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP corrected fore and aft position with the three PCL movements, holding airspeed excursions to about 20 knots, at the edge of the standard, due to the stopping movement being applied a beat after the reference was reached rather than as it was reached. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the stopping movement as the reference is reached, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP corrected fore and aft position with the three PCL movements, holding airspeed excursions to about 15 knots, due to the stabilizing movement following the stopping movement by a fraction rather than in the same rhythm. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to keep the stabilizing movement in the same rhythm as the stopping one.
texts_at.3: SP corrected fore and aft position with the three PCL movements, holding airspeed excursions to about 10 knots, due to one correction being sized with the whole arm before it was refined to a wrist movement. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size every correction with the wrist from the first movement.

texts_above.1: SP corrected fore and aft position with the three PCL movements, holding airspeed excursions to about 18 knots, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP corrected fore and aft position with the three PCL movements, one to start the correction, one to stop the aircraft and one to stabilize it, airspeed excursions held to about 15 knots with power changed in small movements of the wrist rather than the whole arm. Sizing every correction with the wrist from the first movement would remove the last overshoot. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent power-correction discipline.
texts_above.3: SP corrected fore and aft position with the three PCL movements, airspeed excursions held to about 8 knots with the aircraft settling on the reference without overshoot. The only refinement available was to hold that same wrist discipline through the fastest closure of the route. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined power-correction discipline.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the power required and made corrections so small that the fore-and-aft reference never developed a visible error, airspeed effectively constant with every correction started, stopped and stabilized deliberately and no chasing of the power occurring at any stage of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless power-correction discipline.

error_modes.label: ECHELON TURN - ROLL RATE NOT MATCHED AND PLANE OF MOTION NOT HELD

texts.0: SP, due to a roll rate that was not matched to Number 1 at the turning point, did not remain in the same plane of motion and did not keep the horizon bisecting Number 1 fuselage, so the aircraft went high and acute in the turn. Back pressure was used in place of bank to correct the vertical position and the resulting excursion exceeded 400 feet from the briefed level with the flight path no longer deconflicted. The developing sight picture error was not recognized by SP. IP had to take the controls and re-establish safe separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a roll rate lagging Number 1 into the echelon turn, did not hold the plane of motion and allowed the sight picture to break down, with the horizon well off the correct point on Number 1 fuselage. Altitude excursions relative to the briefed level reached 300 feet and the position was restored only after repeated calls. Bank was still not used as the primary means of correcting the vertical position.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed match of Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in, did not hold the vertical position early in the turn and allowed about 200 feet of excursion before recognizing the error. SP corrected the vertical position with bank, the fore and aft position with power and the spacing with back pressure, and re-established the sight picture inside the turn without any call. The roll-out was flown matching Number 1 roll rate.
texts.3: SP matched Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in and the roll-out and maintained the same plane of motion throughout each echelon turn, keeping the horizon bisecting Number 1 fuselage. Vertical excursions stayed within 150 feet and spacing was held with back pressure. Corrections used bank for vertical and power for fore and aft as required.
texts.4: SP matched Number 1 roll rate exactly and held the plane of motion through every turn, so the sight picture remained constant from roll-in to roll-out. Vertical and spacing errors were negligible and no correction was visible from outside. Back pressure was blended smoothly with bank throughout the turn.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within standards through the echelon turns, but the roll rate was matched slightly late at each roll-in and the plane of motion was recovered rather than held. The trend is a reactive rather than an anticipated roll, so the vertical position drifts toward the edge of tolerance in the first part of every turn. SP is expected to match Number 1 roll rate from the initiation of the roll and to keep the horizon bisecting the fuselage on the next formation navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the echelon turn with IP calling when to match Number 1's roll rate and confirming the sight picture through the roll-in, due to this being one of the first echelon turns SP has flown matching roll rate to hold the plane of motion. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to match more of the roll rate independently at the roll-in on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP matched Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in, holding vertical excursions to about 300 feet, at the edge of the standard, due to the roll rate being matched a beat after Number 1 initiated it rather than from the initiation itself. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to match the roll rate from the initiation of the roll, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP matched Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in, holding vertical excursions to about 210 feet, due to the vertical position being corrected with back pressure before bank was used as the primary means. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to use bank as the primary means of correcting the vertical position, not back pressure.
texts_at.3: SP matched Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in, holding vertical excursions to about 150 feet, due to the sight picture being confirmed a fraction after the roll-in rather than through it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the sight picture through the roll-in itself, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP matched Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in, holding vertical excursions to about 280 feet, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP matched Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in and the roll-out and maintained the same plane of motion throughout each echelon turn, vertical excursions held to about 200 feet with spacing held by back pressure and corrections using bank for vertical and power for fore and aft as required. Confirming the sight picture through the roll-in itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the vertical hold further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to good roll-rate-matching discipline.
texts_above.3: SP matched Number 1 roll rate at the roll-in and the roll-out and maintained the same plane of motion, vertical excursions held to about 130 feet with the horizon kept bisecting Number 1's fuselage throughout. The only refinement available was to hold that same match through the fastest roll rate flown. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to very good roll-rate-matching discipline.
texts_above.4: SP matched Number 1 roll rate exactly and held the plane of motion through every turn, so the sight picture remained constant from roll-in to roll-out, vertical and spacing errors negligible with no correction visible from outside and back pressure blended smoothly with bank throughout the turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent roll-rate-matching discipline.
